text.p: Continuing softness in the Australian economy is expected to have kept import demand reasonably flat in September, economists said.
A slight rise in line with expectations, similar to the 1.1 percent seen in August, would keep imports tracking sideways, economists said.
While the moderation seen in the current account deficit has taken some of the heat out of the imports release, it still remains an important indicator of the health of the economy.
The median forecast of the 31 economists surveyed by Reuters was for a 1.0 percent rise in September imports.
Forecasts ranged from a fall of 3.0 percent to a 5.0 percent rise. Six economists forecast a fall.

The expected rise was not a sign of recovering demand as it would still leave imports below their June level, economists said. Instead, it was seen as more just a correction to the recent run of weaker monthly numbers.

Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said that while the imports data was a key input to current account forecasts, "in today's context they are used as an indicator of the health of the economy."
"The current weakness of imports is a reflection of the weakness of the economy rather than a subsitution towards home produced goods," he said.

Of the three import categories, the most closely watched will be capital goods. Capital goods are an important component of business investment, and business investment has been forecast to rise by 14 percent in the year to June 30 1997.

"After falling by over 13 percent in the three months to August a strong kick back in September will be required to stop question marks starting to appear next to Treasury's forecast of 14 percent business investment growth over 1996/97," Commonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney said.
Investment is seen as underpinning the government's economic growth forecast of 3.25 percent, so signs of weakness would raise concerns over growth prospects.
Capital goods imports rose 4.3 percent in August, due totally to the inclusion of an AS96 million plane, but had fallen heavily in the previous two months.
Some economists were expecting a smaller plane, valued at around A$60 million, to be included in the September data.
The Commonwealth Bank economists were among those including the plane, and they were expecting a 5.0 percent rise in total imports, led by capital good imports.
